title: How a name becomes an address
summary: What /etc/hosts, systemd-resolved, nsswitch and a DNS server each actually do, and which one to blame when a name will not resolve.
analogy: Before you can post a letter you need an address. The hosts file is a scribbled note of one address. The resolver is the phone book. systemd-resolved is the receptionist who decides which phone book to open.

related.label: Where the DNS server setting actually comes from
Option 6 handing out a DNS server

sections.h: The order a name is looked up in
p: On RHEL 9 and 10 the answer is not simply "the hosts file, then DNS". The order is controlled by `/etc/nsswitch.conf`, and systemd-resolved sits in the middle of it.
sections.code:
getent hosts example.lab
cat /etc/nsswitch.conf | grep '^hosts:'
resolvectl status
ls -l /etc/resolv.conf

sections.h: The four files and what each one really controls
list: `/etc/hosts` — a static local list. Highest priority, and completely bypasses DNS. Useful for lab pinning, and a common cause of "DNS is broken" that is actually a stale hosts entry.
`/etc/nsswitch.conf` — the `hosts:` line decides which sources are consulted and in what order. This is the file that actually controls resolution order.
`/etc/resolv.conf` — the nameserver list. On RHEL with systemd-resolved it is normally a symlink to a stub resolver, and editing it directly is wrong: the next resolvectl command regenerates it.
`/run/systemd/resolve/resolv.conf` — the real upstream list, fed by NetworkManager from the DHCP lease or the connection profile.

p: NetworkManager accepts the DNS configuration that comes from the DHCP lease or the static profile and writes it into systemd-resolved. systemd-resolved caches it and answers queries locally. That is why `/etc/resolv.conf` points at `127.0.0.53` — it is not a real DNS server, it is the local stub.

You can therefore be in a position where the nameserver you *configured* is correct, the resolver has it, and the resolver still cannot reach it. Those are three different failures and `resolvectl` shows you which layer is wrong.
sections.code:
resolvectl status eth0
resolvectl query example.lab
resolvectl statistics
systemctl status systemd-resolved --no-pager

sections.h: Reading the failure instead of guessing
p: Distinguish three failures. They look identical from an application and have completely different fixes.
list: **Name does not resolve at all** — the resolver has no server or no answer. Fix the DNS server or the zone.
**Name resolves to the wrong address** — resolution worked; the data is wrong. Look at the zone, at DNS caching, and at a stale `/etc/hosts` entry.
**Name resolves but the connection times out** — DNS is fine. This is a firewall or routing problem wearing a DNS costume. Many "DNS is broken" tickets are actually `firewalld` or an ACL.

lab.text: Confirm the resolver is running and see what it knows.
lab.expect: `active` and a DNS Servers line for your active interface.

lab.text: Look up a name you know should work.
lab.cmd:
resolvectl query example.lab
dig example.lab
getent hosts example.lab
lab.expect: An address, or a clear NXDOMAIN/SERVFAIL distinction.

lab.text: Prove that /etc/hosts outranks DNS by pinning a name that does not exist in DNS.
lab.cmd:
echo '127.0.0.99 nonexistent.lab' | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts
resolvectl query nonexistent.lab
lab.expect: Returns 127.0.0.99 even though no such record exists upstream. This is why stale hosts entries hide real DNS faults.

lab.text: Remove the entry again so it does not confuse you later.
Test the resolver with a name that must go to the internet, with the firewall temporarily open.
lab.expect: An answer. If dig times out but the port list shows no DNS service rule, add one — this is the classic local failure.

failures.why: Editing /etc/resolv.conf directly and the change disappears.
failures.fix: It is a symlink into `/run`. Configure DNS on the NetworkManager profile or the DHCP scope instead; `nmcli connection modify 'System eth0' ipv4.dns '10.0.0.53' ipv4.dns-search example.lan` survives a reboot.

failures.why: Resolution works for root but not for a service user.
failures.fix: Not a DNS problem. Check the service's sandbox: systemd units with `PrivateUsers=`, `ProtectSystem=` or a `ResolvConf=` override can see a different view. Check `systemctl cat <unit>`.
getent consults NSS, not just DNS. Something in the `hosts:` line of nsswitch.conf is failing, or a module is missing. Compare with `getent ahosts`.

title: Joining a Windows 11 client to a domain, and what to check when it fails
summary: The join command, the five prerequisites that must be true first, and how to diagnose each failure from the error message.
analogy: Joining a domain is like being issued an ID card by an office. The office has to exist, have a directory of who you are, and be reachable. If any of those three fail, you get no card and no useful error message.

related.label: Install AD DS on the server

sections.h: What actually has to be true before the join will work
p: Nearly every failed domain join is one of these five. Check them in order, because each is cheaper to verify than the one after it.
list: **The DNS client is pointed at a domain controller**, not at a router or a public resolver. This is the number one cause and it accounts for most of the rest.
**The domain controller answers on 389 (LDAP) and 88 (Kerberos)** from this machine, and port 53 for DNS.
**Time is synchronised.** Kerberos requires the clocks to be within five minutes of each other. A client whose clock is wrong gets an error about tickets that makes no sense.
**The machine name is unique and valid** — no spaces, 15 characters or fewer.
**A computer account can be created.** Either the account does not already exist, or the join runs as an account with permission to create one.

sections.h: Verifying the prerequisites before you try
p: Test from the client, not from the server. A server that can reach itself proves nothing about whether the client can.
sections.code:
nslookup dc01.example.lan
Test-NetConnection dc01.example.lan -Port 389
Test-NetConnection dc01.example.lan -Port 88
w32tm /query /status
hostname
sections.where: Windows 11 client, normal prompt is fine for all of these

p: There are two ways. Both need a restart afterwards; the difference is only which prompt appears.
sections.code:
# GUI
sysdm.cpl  ->  Computer name -> Change -> Domain -> example.lan

# Command line (requires a restart afterwards)
Add-Computer -DomainName 'example.lan' -Credential (Get-Credential) -Restart

list: **`The specified domain either does not exist or could not be contacted`** — DNS. `nslookup dc01.example.lan` either fails or returns something that is not a domain controller. Check option 6 in the DHCP scope, not the firewall first.
**`The network path was not found` / `0x80070035`** — the DC is resolvable but unreachable. Firewalld has no equivalent here, but a third-party host firewall on the client or DC will do it.
**`The time difference between the client and server is too great`** — Kerberos. `w32tm /resync` on the client, and check that the client is pointed at a real NTP source.

**`The account is not authorized to log on`** — either a pre-created computer object exists in AD with no reset permission for you, or the join account lacks domain-join rights. Check the computer object in `Get-ADComputer -Identity WS11-001`.
**`The specified account name does not exist`** — the credential is wrong, or you passed a local account instead of a domain one. Use `DOMAIN\user` or `user@example.lan`.

lab.text: From the client, confirm you can resolve and reach the domain controller.
lab.expect: Name resolves to the DC's IP, and TcpTestSucceeded is True.

lab.text: Deliberately break DNS and observe the exact error the join produces.
lab.expect: `The specified domain either does not exist or could not be contacted` — proving the error text you will see later really does mean DNS.

lab.text: Put DNS back and join for real.
lab.expect: The client restarts, and the user signs in with a domain account.

lab.text: After the restart, confirm the machine account exists and is enabled.
lab.expect: `nltest` prints a DC name and a GUID with status 0, and `whoami` shows `EXAMPLE\user`.

failures.why: The join succeeds but Group Policy never applies.
failures.fix: The join is not the whole story. Check `gpresult /r` for error codes, and `klist` to confirm the machine account has a Kerberos ticket. A GPO link to a site with no matching subnet is the usual cause.

failures.why: The client can ping the DC but cannot resolve names.
failures.fix: ICMP is allowed and LDAP is not, or vice versa. Test the actual port with Test-NetConnection rather than assuming ping tells you anything.
